content.chapter: Chapter 1: The First Linguistic Study of Turkic
objectives: Define Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk and the term ‘dialect’ in academic English.
Explain the two aims of the work.
Explain what the content shows about Kashgari’s knowledge.
Use while + -ing, as well as, comparable to and the passive.
content.pedagogy: A dense academic opening. Learners unpack a definition, a double aim and an inference about the author (“the content reflects that …”). A three-part chart (definition / aims / what it shows) supports reading.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The work is a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic, not from Arabic to Turkic.
“Comparable to Arabic” means similar in value, not identical.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while + -ing · as well as · comparable to · passive (was compiled)
Notice (Activity 1): while demonstrating that …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *comparable than · *while demonstrate · *as well as he knew.
Use (Activity 4): define a reference work.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: lin-GUIS-tic, com-PILED, mon-u-MEN-tal, DEM-on-strat-ing, COM-pa-ra-ble.
Names: ka-ra-KHA-nid, dî-VÂ-nü lu-GĀ-ti’t-TÜRK.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a dictionary more than a list of words?”
duringReading: First reading: What kind of work is this?
Second reading: complete the chart: definition / aims / what it shows.
Find what the content reflects about Kashgari.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: define a reference work; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is it called the first linguistic study of Turkic?
What two aims does the work have?
What can we infer about Kashgari from the content?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Karakhanid Turkic” and “A Monumental Work” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: literally, linguistic study, Dialect, regional, compiled, comparable to, had a very good command of.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the three headings.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an encyclopedia entry for the work in 70 words, using while + -ing.

expectedResponses: Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first linguistic study of Turkic. It was compiled as a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic and aims to teach Turkic to Arabs while demonstrating that its richness is comparable to Arabic.
content.transferTask: Define a reference work you use.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate the definition, the aims and the inference?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “while + -ing” and one with “as well as”.

objectives: Describe how the Dîvân was written, revised, presented and translated.
List the main contents of the work.
Explain why it can be regarded as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
Use the present perfect passive, after + -ing, subsequently and be regarded as.
content.pedagogy: A factual chapter that links the 11th century with the present day. A timeline (1072 → 1074 → 1077 → today) and a content map help learners see why the conclusion “an encyclopedia of Turkic culture” follows from the evidence.
anticipatedMisconceptions: He presented the work in 1077, three years after he completed it.
“Encyclopedia” here means a work covering nearly every aspect of life, not a modern multi-volume book.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present perfect passive · after + -ing · subsequently · approximately · be regarded as
Notice (Activity 1): has been translated into …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *has translated (for passive meaning) · *regarded like.
Use (Activity 4): a work that travels.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: muk-te-DÎ bi-em-ril-LÂH, UY-ghur, a-zer-bai-JA-ni.
Stress: sub-SE-quent-ly, ap-PROX-i-mate-ly, en-cy-clo-PE-di-a.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do people translate old books into modern languages?”
duringReading: First reading: When was the work written and presented?
Second reading: draw a timeline and a content map.
Find the conclusion of the chapter.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Timeline and content map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a work that travels; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the list of translations tell us about the work today?
Which contents would interest a historian, and which a linguist?
Is “encyclopedia” a fair description? Why?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Translations” and “An Encyclopedia” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: revising, Subsequently, approximately, proverbs, idioms, regarded as.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline with the years marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short review of the Dîvân for a modern reader.

formativeAssessment: Uses the present perfect passive correctly.
expectedResponses: Kashgari began the work in 1072 and, after revising it several times, completed it in 1074. Subsequently, he presented it in Baghdad. It has been translated into eight languages and can be regarded as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
content.transferTask: Write about a book that has been translated into many languages.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the evidence to the conclusion?

exitTicket: Write one present perfect passive sentence about the Dîvân.

objectives: Describe Kashgari’s birth, death, origins and education, with the book’s level of certainty.
Explain his family background.
Evaluate how he presents himself and what supports it.
Use the perfect infinitive, It is generally accepted that and one of the most + adjective.
content.pedagogy: The chapter combines hedged facts, a self-portrait in Kashgari’s own words and evidence about his education. Learners evaluate a claim using evidence from the same chapter, a key B2 reading skill.
anticipatedMisconceptions: He was born in Barsgan and died in Kashgar; learners often mix them up.
The self-description is in quotation marks: it is Kashgari’s view of himself.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be considered to have + past participle · It is generally accepted that · one of the most + adjective
Notice (Activity 1): is considered to have been born …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *is considered to be born in 1008 (for a past event) · *one of the most eloquent person.
Use (Activity 4): evaluate a self-portrait.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: NASR i-LIG KHAN, xin-JIANG, BAR-sgan, TAF-sir, FIQH.
Stress: e-LO-quent, dis-TIN-guished, CON-quer-or.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do authors make readers trust them?”
duringReading: First reading: Where was Kashgari born and where did he die?
Second reading: make a profile: origins / self-portrait / education.
Find evidence for his education.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Profile; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: evaluate a self-portrait; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How certain is the writer about Kashgari’s place of birth?
Which of Kashgari’s claims are supported by the chapter?
Why might a dictionary writer describe himself in this way?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Barsgan” and “Leading Scholars” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: widely known, forefather, conqueror, eloquent, distinguished, leading scholars.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the profile with the three headings.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short biography of Kashgari for a museum, with two hedged sentences.

formativeAssessment: Describes his origins with the right certainty.
expectedResponses: Kashgari is considered to have been born in 1008, and it is generally accepted that he was born in Barsgan. He describes himself as one of the most eloquent Turks, and his education with the leading scholars of his time supports this view.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners support their evaluation with evidence from the chapter?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is considered to have + past participle”.

objectives: Report Kashgari’s views accurately with reporting verbs.
Explain his argument: why a person of reason should learn Turkish.
Name the qualities he praises.
Use there is no better way than to, in order to and worthy of.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is almost entirely in Kashgari’s own words. Learners practice reporting a historical author’s view without adding their own, and they trace the steps of his argument: qualities → power → follow their path → speak their language.
anticipatedMisconceptions: These are Kashgari’s own words, shown in quotation marks; the narrator reports them.
The argument ends with a practical point: speak their language to make your voice heard.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: there is no better way than to · in order to · worthy of · seek refuge · reporting verbs
Notice (Activity 1): there is no better way than to speak …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct reports.
Likely errors: *no better way than speak · *worthy for praise.
Use (Activity 4): why learn a language?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: ad-MI-ra-ble, do-MIN-ion, RIGHT-eous-ness, op-PRES-sion, REF-uge.
Intonation: read the quotation slowly, with a pause after each sentence.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do people learn the language of a powerful or respected group?”
duringReading: First reading: What qualities does Kashgari praise?
Second reading: trace the argument in four steps.
Find his practical conclusion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Argument steps; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: why learn a language?; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which qualities does Kashgari list?
What does he say a person of reason should do?
Why does he say speaking their language is the best way?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Admirable Qualities” and “Their Language” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: worthy of praise, modesty, dominion, dominant, righteousness, oppression, seek refuge.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four argument steps with the first one filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Summarize Kashgari’s argument in three reported sentences.

formativeAssessment: Reports his views with a reporting verb.
Explains the steps of his argument.
Uses there is no better way than to.
expectedResponses: Kashgari writes that the Turks have many qualities worthy of praise, such as modesty and respect for elders. He argues that, to make one’s voice heard and win their hearts, there is no better way than to speak their language.
content.transferTask: Write an argument about why people learn another language.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep Kashgari’s words separate from their own?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “there is no better way than to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses there is no better way than to.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Hadith and the Journey
objectives: Explain what motivated Kashgari’s journey.
Describe the journey: start, length, route and purpose.
Name the dialects he studied.
Use cleft sentences, set out on, until and reporting with that.
content.pedagogy: The chapter connects belief with action: a hadith Kashgari records, his confidence and a long research journey. Cleft sentences show how the writer emphasizes motivation.
anticipatedMisconceptions: He traveled before he reached Baghdad, not after.
The hadith is something Kashgari records in his work; the narrator reports it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: cleft sentences (It was … that …) · set out on · until + clause · states that …, that … and that …
Notice (Activity 1): It was with this belief and confidence that …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *It was with this belief which · *set out to his journey.
Use (Activity 4): what drives a researcher?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: O-ghuz, CHI-gil, YAG-ma, KYR-gyz, TURK-men.
Stress: CON-fi-dence, ma-TE-ri-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes someone travel for years to research something?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did Kashgari set out on his journey?
Second reading: make a journey card: belief / start / length / result.
Find the six groups whose dialects he learned.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Journey card; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: what drives a researcher?; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the writer link the hadith with the journey?
Why did Kashgari visit so many tribes?
What does “the speech of every tribe” suggest about his method?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “1057” and “Many Dialects” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: long-lasting, confidence, set out on, gathered the material.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the journey card with the start year filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a diary entry by Kashgari halfway through his journey.

expectedResponses: It was with belief and confidence that Kashgari set out on his journey in 1057. For ten to fifteen years, until he reached Baghdad, he traveled from tribe to tribe and gathered the material he needed.
content.transferTask: Write about a person whose belief drove a long project.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the link between belief and action?

exitTicket: Write one cleft sentence about Kashgari’s journey.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: The Oghuz and the Caliph
objectives: Explain why the Oghuz receive the most attention in the work.
Analyze the significance of completing the work in Baghdad.
Name the three great Turkic states of the time.
Use the past perfect, not limited to, The fact that … and namely.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from description to political interpretation. Learners separate facts (twenty-two tribes, Baghdad) from interpretation (“likely reason”, “was likely aware”), a central B2 skill.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The writer says “likely”; the reason is an interpretation, not a proven fact.
The Seljuks protected the Abbasids; the Abbasids did not protect the Seljuks.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past perfect · not limited to · The fact that … holds significance · namely · likely
Notice (Activity 1): had taken the Abbasids … under their protection.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *not limited with · *The fact which …
Use (Activity 4): analyze an author’s choice.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: O-ghuz, SEL-juks, GHAZ-na-vids, ab-BA-sids.
Stress: sig-NIF-i-cance, IN-flu-ence, TRI-bal.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why might an author write more about one group than another?”
duringReading: First reading: Which tribe receives the most attention?
Second reading: make a two-column chart: fact / interpretation.
Find the three great Turkic states.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Fact / interpretation chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: analyze an author’s choice; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which sentences in the chapter are facts, and which are interpretations?
Why does the place where the work was completed matter?
How sure is the writer about Kashgari’s political awareness?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Oghuz” and “Baghdad” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: receives the most attention, not limited to, tribal organization, influence, significance, aware of.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one example in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing the roles of the three great Turkic states, using only the chapter.

expectedResponses: The Oghuz receive the most attention in the work. The likely reason is that the Seljuks, an Oghuz tribe, had taken the Abbasids under their protection. The fact that the work was completed in Baghdad and presented to the caliph holds special significance.
content.transferTask: Analyze why an author might focus on one group.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep facts and interpretations apart?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “The fact that” and one with the past perfect.

objectives: Explain the linguistic situation in the madrasas of the time.
Explain what likely inspired Kashgari to praise Turkish.
Analyze how the writer presents Kashgari’s motivation.
Use in the face of, driven by, inspire someone to and It is likely that.
content.pedagogy: A short chapter with a strong cause → motivation → action structure. It invites learners to think about language status today while keeping respect for every language.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Kashgari did not reject Arabic; he wrote in a world where Arabic was dominant and wanted to show that Turkish could rival it.
“Rival” here is a verb: to be as good as.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in the face of · driven by (participle phrase) · inspire someone to + verb · It is likely that
Notice (Activity 1): driven by a belief in …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *inspired him praising · *in the face to.
Use (Activity 4): a language in the face of change.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: in-STRUC-tion, DOM-i-nance, RI-val, NA-tive.
Linking: “in the face of” /ɪn ðə ˈfeɪs əv/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which languages are dominant in science and the internet today?”
duringReading: First reading: Which language was dominant in the madrasas?
Second reading: draw cause → motivation → action.
Find how sure the writer is.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Cause chain; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: a language in the face of change; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was Arabic the primary language of instruction?
How does the writer show that the motivation is an interpretation?
Can a language rival another without rejecting it?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Madrasas” and “His Native Language” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: primary language of instruction, native language, In the face of, driven by, rival.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the cause chain with the first box filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short speech by Kashgari to the scholars of Baghdad.

formativeAssessment: Uses driven by or in the face of correctly.
expectedResponses: Arabic was the primary language of instruction, and scholars wrote their works in Arabic. In the face of this dominance, Kashgari wrote his work, driven by a belief that his mother tongue could rival Arabic.
content.transferTask: Write about protecting a language in the face of a dominant one.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners show respect for both languages?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “in the face of” and one with “driven by”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses driven by or in the face of.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: The Importance of the Map
objectives: Describe Kashgari’s map: design, colors, center and limits.
Explain how the map reflects his belief.
Explain why the map is important: Japan and the Turkic perspective.
Use not only … but also, owing to, identified as and referred to as.
content.pedagogy: The chapter describes a map and interprets it. Learners build the map on the board while reading, then discuss how a map can show a point of view. The writer’s interpretation (“It is likely that”) is kept separate from the description.
anticipatedMisconceptions: ‘Jabarqa’ is Japan; ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc’ is China.
The second map showing Japan came about four centuries later, not before.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not only … but also · owing to · be identified as / referred to as · is placed / is positioned
Notice (Activity 1): not only described … but also pointed out …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *not only … but too · *referred as.
Use (Activity 4): maps and points of view.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ba-la-sa-GUN, ja-BAR-qa, I-dil, e-thi-O-pi-a.
Stress: car-TOG-ra-pher, CIR-cu-lar, de-PICT, in-HAB-it-ed.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can a map tell us about the person who made it?”
duringReading: First reading: What is at the center of the map?
Second reading: draw the map with its colors and limits.
Find why the map is important today.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–20 Draw the map; 20–23 Quick Challenge; 23–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–42 Use: maps and points of view; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Kashgari widely recognized as the first Turkic cartographer?
How does the map reflect his belief?
What does the map show about the nations that interacted with the Turks?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Center of the World” and “Jabarqa” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: inhabited, Owing to, cartographer, circular, depict.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a circle with the center and directions marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a museum label of 80 words for the map.

formativeAssessment: Explains the link with his belief.
Uses not only … but also correctly.
expectedResponses: Kashgari not only described the geography of the Turkic tribes but also showed it on a circular map. Turkestan is at the center, and the map extends from the Russian border to Japan. Owing to this map, he is recognized as the first Turkic cartographer.
content.transferTask: Write about how a map can reflect a point of view.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the map as both a document and a point of view?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not only … but also” about the map.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the link with his belief.

content.chapter: Chapter 9: The Story of the Calendar
objectives: Retell the legend of the calendar in a formal register.
Explain the khan’s reasoning in his speech.
Describe how the people took part in the decision and the hunt.
Use the first conditional, let us / let this, prior to and participle clauses.
content.pedagogy: A legend told in formal language. The khan’s speech is a model of a proposal: risk → solution → benefit. The people approve and take part, so the calendar becomes a shared record. Present it as a legend that Kashgari records.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The khan did not choose the animals; the order in which they crossed gave the years their names.
A kurultay was a national meeting, not a battle.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: first conditional · let us / let + noun + verb · prior to · participle clause (Starting with …)
Notice (Activity 1): If we are mistaken …, those who come after us will also be mistaken.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *If we will be mistaken · *Let this system serves.
Use (Activity 4): a formal proposal.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: KHAN, ku-rul-TAY, I-li VAL-ley, ka-zakh-STAN.
Stress: con-SULT-ed, mis-TAK-en, ap-PROVED, SUB-se-quent.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do societies need shared calendars?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did the khan want a new system?
Second reading: put five events in order.
Find how the people took part.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Story order; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a formal proposal; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the Turks use this system to record?
What is the structure of the khan’s speech?
Why is it important that the people approved of the idea?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Kurultay” and “The Ili Valley” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: emerged, prior to, reign, consulted, mistaken, approved of.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the five events on cards to order.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite the khan’s speech as a modern formal proposal.

expectedResponses: When people disagreed on the date of an old battle, the khan gathered a kurultay. He argued that if they were mistaken, future generations would be too, so he proposed a twelve-year system. Starting with the rat, the years were named after the animals that crossed the river.
content.transferTask: Write a formal proposal for a system at your school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the speech as a model of a proposal?

exitTicket: Write one first conditional sentence and one sentence with “Let …”.

objectives: Name the twelve years in order.
Match old Turkic names with English meanings.
Explain how the list reflects Kashgari’s dictionary method.
Use ordinal numbers and defining patterns.
content.pedagogy: A list chapter at B2 is a chance to discuss method: Kashgari records a word and gives its meaning, which is exactly what the list does. Learners then write their own entries. Keep the old names as they are in the book.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Nag means ‘Crocodile’ in this list; keep the book’s meaning.
Spelling: fifth, ninth, twelfth.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: ordinal numbers · X means Y · defining patterns for dictionary entries
Notice (Activity 1): Year of the Nag means ‘Year of the Crocodile’.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose ordinals, then sort the animals.
Likely errors: *fiveth · *nineth · *the five year.
Use (Activity 4): write dictionary entries.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Ordinals: fifth /fɪfθ/, ninth /naɪnθ/, twelfth /twelfθ/.
Old names: sıç-GAN, ta-vış-GAN, ta-ka-GU, toŋ-GUZ.
beforeReading: Ask: “What information does a good dictionary entry give?”
duringReading: First reading: How many years are in the cycle?
Second reading: underline the old names you can guess.
Find the animals in the first and second halves.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Underline and guess; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: dictionary entries; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which old names are close to modern Turkish words?
How does the list show Kashgari’s method?
Why are old words worth recording?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The First Year” and “The Last Year” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give picture cards of the twelve animals.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the twelve years in order with ordinal numbers, old names and meanings.

expectedResponses: The cycle begins with the Year of the Sıçgan, which means ‘Year of the Rat’, and ends with the twelfth year, the Year of the Toŋguz, which means ‘Year of the Pig’.
content.transferTask: Write dictionary entries for old or regional words.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the list with the method of the whole work?

objectives: Explain the beliefs linked with the Years of the Ox, Rooster, Snake, Crocodile and Pig, with the reasons given.
Describe how the calendar measures time: cycle, year, month, day and çağ.
Distinguish reported beliefs from descriptions of the system.
Use some …, while others …, known for, derive from and participle clauses.
content.pedagogy: The chapter reports beliefs (“they say”, “they make predictions”) and then describes the system of time. Keep both clearly as information that Kashgari records about the old calendar.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The beliefs are old beliefs reported in the book, not predictions for today.
A cycle lasts 12 years; a çağ lasts two hours.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: some …, while others … · known for + -ing · derive meaning from · participle clause of result (meaning …) · when + present
Notice (Activity 1): some years are considered prosperous, while others …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *known as butting · *derive meanings of it.
Use (Activity 4): explaining a traditional belief.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: PROS-per-ous, a-BUN-dant, dis-OR-der, fer-TIL-i-ty, HAB-i-tat.
Word: çağ /tʃaː/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why did people in the past link years or seasons with good or bad events?”
duringReading: First reading: Which years are prosperous and which are tough?
Second reading: make a chart: year / belief / reason given.
Find how the calendar divides a day.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a traditional belief; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What reasons are given for the beliefs about each year?
How do the beliefs connect animals with nature?
How does the calendar divide time?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Year of the Ox” and “Twelve Parts of a Day” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: prosperous, butting, abundant, disorder, fertility, natural habitat, resets.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the Year of the Ox filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing two years of the calendar, using while and known for.

formativeAssessment: Explains two beliefs with their reasons.
Describes how the calendar measures time.
Uses while or known for correctly.
expectedResponses: Some years are considered prosperous, while others are considered tough. The Year of the Ox is linked with more wars because the ox is known for butting. A day is divided into twelve parts, meaning each çağ lasts two hours.
content.transferTask: Explain a traditional belief from your region.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners treat the beliefs as reported information?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “some …, while others …”.

objectives: Use the Orkhon Inscriptions as evidence for the long use of the calendar.
Explain the role of Nowruz in the calendar and today.
Distinguish known facts from description.
Use It is known that, that is, which (non-defining) and the present perfect.
content.pedagogy: The chapter turns from beliefs to evidence. The Orkhon Inscriptions date events with the calendar centuries before Kashgari, and Nowruz links the old calendar with a living tradition.

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk (Kaşgarlı Mahmud)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 14 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended texts about history, language and culture, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations, evaluations and arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Mahmud Kashgari and Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk: the work and its aims, the author’s life, words and journey, the Oghuz and the caliph, the map, the Twelve-Animal calendar, the Orkhon evidence, excerpts from the Dîvân and its legacy, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (It is known that / is considered to have been / It is likely that) and separates reported words from narration, and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 14 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definition, timeline, quotation and argument, interpretation, legend, list, evidence or excerpt.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include the perfect infinitive, the present perfect passive, cleft sentences, participle clauses, not only … but also and formal linkers. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: while + -ing · as well as · comparable to · passive (was compiled)
Ch2: present perfect passive · after + -ing · subsequently · approximately · be regarded as
Ch3: be considered to have + past participle · It is generally accepted that · one of the most + adjective
Ch4: there is no better way than to · in order to · worthy of · seek refuge · reporting verbs
Ch5: cleft sentences (It was … that …) · set out on · until + clause · states that …, that … and that …
Ch6: past perfect · not limited to · The fact that … holds significance · namely · likely
Ch7: in the face of · driven by (participle phrase) · inspire someone to + verb · It is likely that
Ch8: not only … but also · owing to · be identified as / referred to as · is placed / is positioned
Ch9: first conditional · let us / let + noun + verb · prior to · participle clause (Starting with …)
Ch10: ordinal numbers · X means Y · defining patterns for dictionary entries
Ch11: some …, while others … · known for + -ing · derive meaning from · participle clause of result (meaning …) · when + present
Ch12: It is known that · that is (= in other words) · non-defining which · present perfect with since
Ch13: As the proverb goes · let + person + base verb · so that … may · allow someone to + verb
Ch14: present perfect passive · gain someone something · date back to · is kept · be regarded as

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow extended narration for gist, attributed views and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify definitions, timelines, arguments, degrees of certainty, interpretations and evidence.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain and evaluate, attribute views, compare past and present and present balanced positions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce clear, detailed B2 paragraphs and short arguments with evidence, hedging and balanced conclusions.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for elders, for scholars and for every language.
D3 Diligence — Long, patient work to reach a goal.
D16 Responsibility — Thinking about the people who come after us.
languageFocus: Every one of the 14 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for evaluation, counterpoints and evidence from more than one chapter, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Chapter 4 is in Kashgari’s own words. Read the sentences about Allah and the Turks as his quoted words, without extra comment, and keep them separate from the narrator.
The hadith in Chapter 5 is something Kashgari records in his work; it is read as it is.
The beliefs about the meaning of each year belong to the old Turkic calendar; present them as old beliefs, not as predictions for today.
Chapters 6, 7 and 8 use “likely”; present these as the writer’s interpretations, not as proven facts.
The Old Turkic proverb and poem lines and the bracketed Turkish words belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Mahmud Kashgari’s dictionary links the 11th-century Turkic world with questions every community faces today: how to keep a language alive, how to record shared time and how to learn about other nations.

themes.title: Keeping a language alive:
themes.description: Kashgari recorded words, proverbs and poems from many tribes (Chapters 2, 5 and 13). Discuss how people protect languages and dialects today.

themes.title: Shared time:
themes.description: The khan consulted his people and created a shared calendar (Chapter 9). Compare calendars and new year days, such as Nowruz (Chapter 12).

themes.title: Maps and points of view:
themes.description: Kashgari placed the Turkic homeland at the center of his map (Chapter 8). Discuss how maps can reflect a point of view.

themes.title: Shared heritage:
themes.description: Many countries supported the UNESCO commemoration (Chapter 14). Discuss how nations can share a cultural heritage.

miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an expert: biographer, linguist, historian or calendar expert. Prepare a two-minute statement with one quotation, hold a panel discussion and agree on the most important legacy of the Dîvân today.

reflectivePrompt.title: Language, Memory and Identity
reflectivePrompt.desc: Kashgari recorded the words, proverbs and traditions of many Turkic tribes (Chapters 2, 5 and 13). Write eight to ten sentences arguing why communities record their languages and traditions. Use evidence from the book and one counterpoint.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Kashgari praises respect for elders, studied under the leading scholars of his time and mastered Arabic and Persian while praising Turkish (Chapters 1, 3, 4 and 7).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Kashgari revised his work several times and traveled for ten to fifteen years to gather his material (Chapters 2 and 5).

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The khan consulted his people and created a calendar so that future generations would not be mistaken (Chapter 9).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: The poem in the Dîvân advises letting others enjoy the delicious food and entertaining the guest (Chapter 13).

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study Mahmud Kashgari and Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 14 chapters of Mahmud Kashgari.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the aims, contents and historical setting of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk.
Evaluate its map, calendar, excerpts and legacy with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 14.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea from the Dîvân that I think is still relevant today, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 14 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, diligence, responsibility and generosity. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Kashgari praises respect for elders, studied under the leading scholars of his time and mastered Arabic and Persian while praising Turkish (Chapters 1, 3, 4 and 7).
Diligence: Diligence: Kashgari revised his work several times and traveled for ten to fifteen years to gather his material (Chapters 2 and 5).
Responsibility: Responsibility: The khan consulted his people and created a calendar so that future generations would not be mistaken (Chapter 9).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: The poem in the Dîvân advises letting others enjoy the delicious food and entertaining the guest (Chapter 13).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 14, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Explain to someone at home in six sentences who Mahmud Kashgari was and why his work still matters, in your home language or in English.
